claims.text: A defect-aware predictive approach will predict thermal transport in bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal models.
A defect-aware predictive approach will predict electrical transport in bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal models.
The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
The target material has a typical distribution of intrinsic defects.
The proposed hybrid framework explicitly represents oxygen impurities and associated defect clusters.
The proposed applicability ranges are 0–200 K and 300–1200 K under equilibrium conditions.
Oxygen impurities induce defect clusters and local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-associated defects and distortions scatter phonons.
The oxygen-associated defects and distortions scatter electrons.
Reduced phonon populations at low temperature cause oxygen-cluster defect scattering to dominate transport behavior.
Defect scattering produces larger deviations from perfect-crystal predictions at low temperatures than at high temperatures.
Intrinsic phonon–phonon interactions increase at high temperatures.
Increasing phonon–phonon interactions make the relative contribution of defect scattering less pronounced at high temperatures.
Including realistic defect configurations allows the proposed approach to capture competing defect and intrinsic scattering mechanisms.
At cryogenic temperatures, the defect-aware prediction will be approximately 15–20% below the perfect-crystal conductivity value.
At high temperatures, the defect-aware prediction will be approximately 5–10% below the perfect-crystal conductivity value.
Conventional analytical transport models for this comparison assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Ignoring defects causes substantial transport-prediction errors, particularly at low temperature.
The hypothesis is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The hypothesis may not apply to substantially higher oxygen concentrations or to non-equilibrium processing conditions with markedly different defect distributions.
